statement: The [excursions](c:excursion) of a [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) away from 0, labelled by the [local time](c:local-time) at 0, form a [Poisson random measure](c:poisson-random-measure) with intensity Lebesgue measure times a σ-finite measure $n$, the excursion measure.

hypotheses.text: $B$ is a standard linear [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) with $B_0 = 0$.
$L_t$ is the [local time](c:local-time) of $B$ at 0, normalized so that $|B_t| - L_t$ is a martingale.

conclusion: The excursion point process $\Xi = \sum_\ell \delta_{(\ell, e_\ell)}$ is Poisson with intensity $d\ell \otimes n(de)$. Here $n(U) = \infty$ and $n(\sup f > a) = n(\inf f < -a) = 1/(2a)$ for $a > 0$.

proofs.name: Regeneration at inverse local times
proofs.slogan: The strong Markov property at inverse local times makes each excursion count a Poisson process, and Itô's criterion gives the joint Poisson law.
proofs.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of THEOREM (Ito) and Proposition 2 in Rogers (1989), pp. 313-314, completed by Theorem 3.1 and Section 4 of Itô (1972).

roles.why: The strong Markov property of Brownian motion restarts the path at each inverse local time.
The local time labels the excursions, and its normalization fixes the value of the excursion measure.

steps.slogan: Label each excursion by the value of the local time during it.
steps.detail: The inverse $\gamma_\ell = \inf\{u : L_u > \ell\}$ is a [stopping time](c:stopping-time) with $B(\gamma_\ell) = 0$. Its jumps $(\gamma_{\ell-}, \gamma_\ell)$ are exactly the excursion intervals, so each excursion gets one label $\ell$.

steps.slogan: Restart the Brownian motion at each inverse local time by the strong Markov property.
steps.detail: The path $B(\gamma_\ell + \cdot)$ is a Brownian motion from 0 and is independent of the path before $\gamma_\ell$. So the excursions with labels after $\ell$ are independent of the earlier ones and have the same law as all excursions.

steps.slogan: Show that each count of long excursions is a Poisson process in local time.
steps.detail: Before $\gamma_t$ at most $m\gamma_t$ excursions last longer than $1/m$. For $A \subset \{\zeta > 1/m\}$ the count $\Xi((0,t] \times A)$ is finite, has stationary [independent increments](c:independent-increments) and moves by unit jumps, so it is a [Poisson process](c:poisson-process).

steps.slogan: Combine the counts of disjoint sets into one jump process with independent Poisson jump counts.
steps.detail: For disjoint $E_1, \dots, E_k$, Itô's process $Z^* = \sum_i i Z_i$ has independent increments and jumps of sizes $1, \dots, k$. Its numbers of jumps of each size are independent Poisson variables, and $Z_i$ counts the jumps of size $i$.

steps.slogan: Identify the mean measure as Lebesgue measure times the excursion measure.
steps.detail: The mean $M(E) = E\,\Xi(E)$ is a measure that does not change under shifts of the label. It is finite on $(0,t] \times \{\zeta > 1/m\}$, so $M = d\ell \otimes n$ with a [σ-finite measure](c:sigma-finite-measure) $n$.

steps.slogan: Compute the measure of high excursions by optional stopping for |B| − L.
steps.detail: The first excursion with $\sup |f| > a$ has the label $L_H$ for $H = \inf\{t : |B_t| = a\}$, so $E L_H = 1/n(\sup|f| > a)$. The [martingale](c:martingale) $|B| - L$ gives $E L_H = a$. Symmetry splits $1/a$ into two halves $1/(2a)$.

concepts.c:excursion: The theorem describes the law of all excursions of the path from 0.
concepts.c:brownian-motion: Brownian motion is the process whose excursions the theorem describes.
concepts.c:local-time: The local time at 0 is the clock that labels the excursions.
concepts.c:poisson-random-measure: The labelled excursions form a Poisson random measure on labels times excursions.
concepts.c:stopping-time: Each inverse local time is a stopping time, so the strong Markov property applies there.
concepts.c:independent-increments: Regeneration gives each excursion count independent and stationary increments.
concepts.c:poisson-process: A counting process with stationary independent increments and unit jumps is a Poisson process.
concepts.c:sigma-finite-measure: The excursion measure is σ-finite but infinite, because small excursions are countless.
concepts.c:martingale: Optional stopping for the martingale |B| − L computes the excursion measure.

source.ref: L. C. G. Rogers, A guided tour through excursions, Bull. London Math. Soc. 21 (1989), THEOREM (Ito) and its proof, p. 313, and Proposition 2, p. 314.
source.note: Rogers proves the renewal property and the Poisson law of one count, and refers to Itô for the rest. The joint law and the product intensity follow K. Itô, Poisson point processes attached to Markov processes (1972), Theorem 3.1 and Section 4.

new_concepts.name: excursion
new_concepts.reminder: An excursion of a process away from $0$ is the piece of path between two consecutive visits to $0$.
new_concepts.definition: Let $X$ be a real [stochastic process](c:stochastic-process) with continuous paths and $X_0=0$, such as [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion), with zero set $Z=\{t:X_t=0\}$. For each connected component $(g,d)$ of the open set $(0,\infty)\setminus Z$ with $d<\infty$, the excursion on $(g,d)$ is the path piece $e(s)=X_{g+s}$, $0\le s\le d-g$, which leaves $0$ at time $g$ and returns at time $d$. For a [random walk](c:random-walk) on $\mathbb{Z}$, an excursion is the path between two consecutive visits to $0$.

new_concepts.name: local time
new_concepts.reminder: The local time $L_t^x$ measures how much time a process spends near the level $x$ up to time $t$.
new_concepts.definition: For a one-dimensional [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) $B$, the local time is the jointly continuous process $(L_t^x)_{t\ge0,x\in\mathbb{R}}$ such that $\int_0^tf(B_s)\,ds=\int_{\mathbb{R}}f(x)L_t^x\,dx$ for all bounded Borel functions $f$ and all $t$, almost surely. So $x\mapsto L_t^x$ is the [Radon–Nikodym derivative](c:radon-nikodym-derivative) of the occupation measure $A\mapsto\int_0^t1_A(B_s)\,ds$ with respect to [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure). For a continuous [semimartingale](c:semimartingale) $X$, the same formula with $d\langle X\rangle_s$ in place of $ds$ defines $L_t^x$, which is then right-continuous in $x$.

new_concepts.name: point process
new_concepts.reminder: A point process is a random locally finite set of points, described by the random counts it puts in sets.
new_concepts.definition: Let $E$ be a locally compact Hausdorff space with a countable base, and let $M_p(E)$ be the set of [Radon measures](c:radon-measure) on $E$ with values in $\{0,1,2,\dots,\infty\}$, which are the locally finite sums of [Dirac measures](c:dirac-measure). A point process on $E$ is a [random variable](c:random-variable) $N$ with values in $M_p(E)$, where $M_p(E)$ has the sigma-algebra generated by the maps $\mu\mapsto\mu(B)$ for Borel sets $B$. Each count $N(B)$ is then a random variable, and it is finite when $B$ is relatively compact.

new_concepts.name: Poisson random measure
new_concepts.reminder: A Poisson random measure puts independent Poisson numbers of points in disjoint sets, with means given by a fixed measure.
new_concepts.definition: Let $\mu$ be a [sigma-finite measure](c:sigma-finite-measure) on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal{E})$. A Poisson random measure with mean measure $\mu$ is a random measure $N$ on $E$ with values in $\{0,1,2,\dots,\infty\}$ such that $N(B)$ has the [Poisson distribution](c:poisson-distribution) with mean $\mu(B)$ for each $B$ with $\mu(B)<\infty$, and $N(B_1),\dots,N(B_k)$ are [independent random variables](c:independent-random-variables) for disjoint $B_1,\dots,B_k$. Such an $N$ exists for every sigma-finite $\mu$, and $\mu$ determines its law.

statement: For a standard [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) $B$, the last zero $L$ of $B$ in $[0,1]$ and the a.s. unique time $M^*$ of the maximum of $B$ on $[0,1]$ both have the arcsine [distribution function](c:distribution-function) $\frac{2}{\pi}\arcsin\sqrt{s}$.

hypotheses.text: $B$ is a standard linear [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) with $B(0) = 0$, continuous paths and [independent increments](c:independent-increments) $B(t) - B(r) \sim N(0, t - r)$.

conclusion: $P(L \le s) = P(M^* \le s) = \frac{2}{\pi}\arcsin\sqrt{s}$ for $s \in [0,1]$, with [density](c:probability-density-function) $\frac{1}{\pi\sqrt{s(1-s)}}$ on $(0,1)$.

proofs.name: Time reversal at s and polar coordinates
proofs.slogan: Split the path at time $s$, compare two independent maxima by the reflection principle, and read the arcsine from a uniform angle.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. Steps 1 to 4 give the law of the maximiser $M^*$. Step 5 moves the law to the last zero $L$ with Lévy's identity.

roles.why: Independent Gaussian increments give the unique maximiser, the independence of the two halves, the reflection principle and the scaling.

steps.slogan: Show that the maximiser of the path on $[0,1]$ is almost surely unique.
steps.detail: For rationals $a < b < c < d$ the difference of the maxima on $[c,d]$ and $[a,b]$ contains the independent [normal](c:normal-distribution) term $B(c) - B(b)$, so it has a continuous law and is zero with probability $0$. A countable union over rational quadruples excludes two maximisers.

steps.slogan: Split the path at time $s$ into a reversed past and an independent future.
steps.detail: The [time reversal](c:time-reversal) $B_1(t) = B(s-t) - B(s)$ has covariance $\min(t,u)$, so it is a Brownian motion on $[0,s]$. The future $B_2(t) = B(s+t) - B(s)$ is an independent Brownian motion. Then $\{M^* < s\} = \{M_1(s) > M_2(1-s)\}$ for the running maxima.

steps.slogan: Replace each running maximum by an absolute Gaussian value with the reflection principle.
steps.detail: The reflection principle gives $M_i(r) \sim |B_i(r)|$, and scaling gives $P(M^* < s) = P(\sqrt{s}\,|Z_1| > \sqrt{1-s}\,|Z_2|) = P(Z_2^2 < s(Z_1^2 + Z_2^2))$ with $Z_1, Z_2$ independent standard normal.

steps.slogan: Compute the probability with the uniform angle of a planar Gaussian vector.
steps.detail: In [polar coordinates](c:polar-coordinates) the density of $(Z_1, Z_2)$ factors as $(2\pi)^{-1} r e^{-r^2/2}\,dr\,d\theta$, so $\theta$ has the [uniform distribution](c:uniform-distribution) on $[0, 2\pi)$. The event $|\sin\theta| < \sqrt{s}$ has angular length $4\arcsin\sqrt{s}$, so $P(M^* \le s) = \frac{2}{\pi}\arcsin\sqrt{s}$.

steps.slogan: Transfer the law from the maximiser to the last zero with Lévy's identity.
steps.detail: The processes $M - B$ and $|B|$ have the same law on $C[0,1]$. The last-zero map $\Lambda(f) = \sup\{t \le 1 : f(t) = 0\}$ is measurable, $\Lambda(|B|) = L$, and $\Lambda(M - B) = M^*$ because the maximiser is unique. Hence $L$ and $M^*$ have the same arcsine law.

concepts.c:brownian-motion: Brownian motion is the process whose last zero and maximiser the theorem describes.
concepts.c:independent-increments: Independent increments make the past and the future of the path at time s independent.
concepts.c:distribution-function: The arcsine distribution function is the conclusion of the theorem.
concepts.c:probability-density-function: The density 1/(π√(s(1−s))) shows that the law is concentrated near 0 and 1.
concepts.c:normal-distribution: Normal increments give continuous laws and the Gaussian pair (Z₁, Z₂).
concepts.c:time-reversal: Reversing the path before time s gives a second Brownian motion.
concepts.c:polar-coordinates: Polar coordinates turn the Gaussian probability into an angle computation.
concepts.c:uniform-distribution: The angle of a standard planar Gaussian vector is uniformly distributed.

source.ref: P. Mörters and Y. Peres, Brownian Motion (Cambridge University Press, 2010, authors' version), Theorem 5.26 and its proof, p. 136.
source.note: The source proves part (b) by time reversal, the reflection principle and polar coordinates, and part (a) by Lévy's theorem on M − B. These steps add the proof of the uniqueness of the maximiser.

statement: Let $B$ be a standard [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) with running maximum $M(t) = \max_{s \le t} B(s)$. Then $2M - B$ is a three-dimensional [Bessel process](c:bessel-process) $\rho$ started at 0. Moreover $(2M - B, M)$ has the same law as $(\rho, I)$, where $I(t) = \inf_{s \ge t} \rho(s)$ is the future infimum.

hypotheses.text: $B$ is a standard linear [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) with $B(0) = 0$.
$\rho = |W|$ for a three-dimensional Brownian motion $W$ with $W(0) = 0$, and $I(t) = \inf_{s \ge t}\rho(s)$.

conclusion: $\{(2M(t) - B(t), M(t)) : t \ge 0\}$ and $\{(\rho(t), I(t)) : t \ge 0\}$ have the same law, so $2M - B$ is a three-dimensional Bessel process.

proofs.name: Discrete Pitman identity and the invariance principle
proofs.slogan: Prove the identity for simple random walk by matching transition probabilities, then pass to Brownian motion by scaling limits.
proofs.scope: Outline of the proof in Mörters and Peres, Section 5.5, with the starting point of the discrete identity corrected.

roles.why: Donsker's theorem makes rescaled simple [random walk](c:random-walk) converge to $B$, so the walk identity passes to $B$.
The radial exit probabilities of three-dimensional Brownian motion make the embedded radius a walk conditioned to avoid zero.

steps.slogan: Compare the walk with its maximum to the conditioned walk with its future minimum.
steps.detail: Let $S$ be simple random walk from 0 and $\tilde\rho$ the [Markov chain](c:markov-chain) on $\{1, 2, \dots\}$ with up-probability $(k+1)/(2k)$, started at 1. The claim is $(2\tilde M - S + 1, \tilde M + 1) \overset{d}{=} (\tilde\rho, \tilde I)$, and $\tilde I$ is the running maximum of $2\tilde I - \tilde\rho$.

steps.slogan: Show that the future minimum is uniform and that both pairs have the same transitions.
steps.detail: The conditioned walk from $k$ reaches $i \le k$ with probability $i/k$, so $\tilde I(j)$ is [uniform](c:uniform-distribution) on $\{1, \dots, k\}$ given $\tilde\rho(j) = k$. [Conditional probability](c:conditional-probability) then gives steps $\pm 1$ with probability $1/2$, exactly as for $(S, \tilde M)$.

steps.slogan: Embed the conditioned walk in a Bessel process at the times when the radius moves by h.
steps.detail: The [stopping times](c:stopping-time) $\tau_j$ when $|x_h + W|$ moves by $h$ give the conditioned walk times $h$. The [martingale](c:martingale) $\rho^2 - 3t$ and Doob's inequality give $\tau_{\lfloor t/h^2 \rfloor} \to t$ uniformly, so the embedded walk converges to $(\rho, I)$.

steps.slogan: Pass to the scaling limit with Donsker's theorem and the continuous mapping theorem.
steps.detail: Rescaled simple random walk converges to $B$, and $f \mapsto (2\max f - f, \max f)$ is continuous, so the left pair [converges in distribution](c:convergence-in-distribution) to $(2M - B, M)$. The right pair converges to $(\rho, I)$, and limits in law are unique.

concepts.c:brownian-motion: The theorem transforms a linear Brownian motion and its maximum.
concepts.c:bessel-process: The radius of three-dimensional Brownian motion is the process that appears.
concepts.c:random-walk: The proof first proves the identity for simple random walk.
concepts.c:markov-chain: The walk conditioned to avoid zero is a Markov chain with explicit transitions.
concepts.c:uniform-distribution: Given the current position, the future minimum is uniform on the levels below.
concepts.c:conditional-probability: The transition probabilities of the pair are ratios of conditional probabilities.
concepts.c:stopping-time: The embedding uses the stopping times when the radius moves by h.
concepts.c:martingale: The martingale rho squared minus 3t controls the embedding times.
concepts.c:convergence-in-distribution: The scaling limit transfers the discrete identity to Brownian motion.

source.ref: P. Mörters and Y. Peres, Brownian Motion, Cambridge University Press 2010, Section 5.5, Lemma 5.31, Lemma 5.32, Proposition 5.33 and Theorem 5.34 with its proof, pp. 140-144.
source.note: The steps follow the source proof. The source states the discrete identity with the conditioned walk started at 0, which fails at time 1. The steps start the conditioned walk at 1 and shift the walk pair by 1, which is Pitman's original discrete form.

new_concepts.name: Bessel process
new_concepts.reminder: The distance from the origin of a Brownian motion in several dimensions.
new_concepts.definition: For an integer $d \ge 1$, the $d$-dimensional Bessel process is $\rho(t) = |W(t)|$, where $W$ is a $d$-dimensional [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion). For $d = 3$ and $\rho(0) = r > 0$ it never hits 0, and it ever reaches a level $a < r$ with probability $a/r$.

statement: For a [martingale](c:martingale) $Y_k$ with $Y_0 = 0$, differences $X_k \le R$ and [predictable](c:predictable-process) quadratic variation $W_k = \sum_{j \le k} \mathbb{E}_{j-1}[X_j^2]$, for all $t \ge 0$ and $\sigma^2 > 0$, $\mathbb{P}(\exists k : Y_k \ge t,\ W_k \le \sigma^2) \le \exp\!\big(-\tfrac{\sigma^2}{R^2} h(\tfrac{Rt}{\sigma^2})\big) \le \exp\!\big(-\tfrac{t^2/2}{\sigma^2 + Rt/3}\big)$ with $h(u) = (1+u)\log(1+u) - u$.

hypotheses.text: $(Y_k)_{k \ge 0}$ is a real [martingale](c:martingale) for a [filtration](c:filtration) $(\mathcal{F}_k)$ with $Y_0 = 0$.
The differences satisfy $X_k = Y_k - Y_{k-1} \le R$ almost surely, with a constant $R > 0$.
The deviation is measured on the event $W_k \le \sigma^2$, where $W_k = \sum_{j \le k} \mathbb{E}[X_j^2 \mid \mathcal{F}_{j-1}]$ is [predictable](c:predictable-process).

conclusion: $\mathbb{P}(\exists k \ge 0 : Y_k \ge t \text{ and } W_k \le \sigma^2) \le \exp\!\big(-\tfrac{\sigma^2}{R^2} h(\tfrac{Rt}{\sigma^2})\big) \le \exp\!\big(-\tfrac{t^2/2}{\sigma^2 + Rt/3}\big)$.

proofs.name: Exponential supermartingale and stopping
proofs.slogan: Compensate the exponential of the martingale by its predictable variance, stop it at the first bad time, and optimize the exponent.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, both the Bennett form and the Bernstein form. The case $t = 0$ is trivial.

roles.why: The zero conditional mean $\mathbb{E}_{k-1}[X_k] = 0$ removes the linear term in the conditional exponential moment.
The one-sided bound $X_k \le R$ lets the exponential be bounded by a quadratic with the coefficient $g(\lambda)$.
On the event $W_\tau \le \sigma^2$ the compensator is at most $g(\lambda)\sigma^2$, which gives the lower bound for the supermartingale.

steps.slogan: Bound the exponential $e^{\lambda x}$ by a quadratic for all $x \le R$.
steps.detail: With $g(\lambda) = (e^{\lambda R} - 1 - \lambda R)/R^2$, the function $(e^y - 1 - y)/y^2 = \int_0^1 (1-s)e^{sy}\,ds$ is nondecreasing, so $e^{\lambda x} \le 1 + \lambda x + g(\lambda)x^2$ for $x \le R$.

steps.slogan: Bound the conditional [moment generating function](c:moment-generating-function) of each increment.
steps.detail: Taking [conditional expectation](c:conditional-expectation) and using $\mathbb{E}_{k-1}[X_k] = 0$ gives $\mathbb{E}_{k-1}[e^{\lambda X_k}] \le 1 + g(\lambda)V_k \le e^{g(\lambda)V_k}$ with $V_k = \mathbb{E}_{k-1}[X_k^2]$.

steps.slogan: Build the compensated exponential process and show that it is a [supermartingale](c:supermartingale).
steps.detail: Since $W_k$ is known at time $k-1$, the process $M_k = \exp(\lambda Y_k - g(\lambda)W_k)$ satisfies $\mathbb{E}_{k-1}[M_k] \le M_{k-1}$, with $M_0 = 1$ and $M_k \ge 0$.

steps.slogan: Stop the supermartingale at the first time the gain is large and the variance small.
steps.detail: For the [stopping time](c:stopping-time) $\tau = \inf\{k : Y_k \ge t,\ W_k \le \sigma^2\}$, optional stopping gives $\mathbb{E}[M_{\tau \wedge n}] \le 1$ and $M_\tau \ge e^{\lambda t - g(\lambda)\sigma^2}$, so $\mathbb{P}(\tau < \infty) \le e^{-\lambda t + g(\lambda)\sigma^2}$.

steps.slogan: Choose the parameter $\lambda$ that minimizes the exponent and compare with the Bernstein form.
steps.detail: The choice $\lambda = R^{-1}\log(1 + Rt/\sigma^2)$ gives the exponent $-(\sigma^2/R^2)h(Rt/\sigma^2)$. Comparing second derivatives, $h''(u) = 1/(1+u) \ge 27/(3+u)^3$, gives $h(u) \ge (u^2/2)/(1 + u/3)$.

concepts.c:martingale: The deviation of a martingale is the object that the inequality bounds.
concepts.c:filtration: The filtration defines what is known at each time and which processes are predictable.
concepts.c:predictable-process: The quadratic variation is predictable, so it can sit inside the exponential compensator.
concepts.c:moment-generating-function: The conditional moment generating function of each increment controls the growth of the exponential process.
concepts.c:conditional-expectation: Conditional expectations given the past define the variance terms and the supermartingale property.
concepts.c:supermartingale: The compensated exponential is a nonnegative supermartingale with initial value one.
concepts.c:stopping-time: The first time of a large gain with small variance is a stopping time where optional stopping applies.

source.ref: J. A. Tropp, Freedman's inequality for matrix martingales, Electron. Commun. Probab. 16 (2011), proofs of Lemma 2.1, Theorem 2.3 and Theorem 3.1, pp. 5-7 (arXiv:1101.3039v1).
source.note: The steps are the scalar case (d = 1) of the source proof, where Lieb's theorem is not needed. The quadratic bound of the exponential and the comparison of h with the Bernstein function are proved here in full.

new_concepts.name: supermartingale
new_concepts.reminder: A supermartingale is an adapted integrable process whose conditional mean of the next value is at most the present value.
new_concepts.definition: An adapted process $(X_n)$ of [integrable](c:integrable-function) random variables for a [filtration](c:filtration) $(\mathcal{F}_n)$ is a supermartingale when the [conditional expectation](c:conditional-expectation) satisfies $\mathbb{E}[X_{n+1}\mid\mathcal{F}_n]\le X_n$ almost surely for every $n$. In continuous time the condition is $\mathbb{E}[X_t\mid\mathcal{F}_s]\le X_s$ for $s\le t$. So a supermartingale decreases on average, and $-X$ is a [submartingale](c:submartingale).

statement: If $B$ is a standard [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) and $T$ is a [stopping time](c:stopping-time), the process $B^*(t) = B(t)$ for $t \le T$ and $B^*(t) = 2B(T) - B(t)$ for $t > T$ is again a standard Brownian motion. For linear $B$ with $M(t) = \max_{s \le t} B(s)$, $a > 0$ and $b \le a$: $\mathbb{P}(M(t) \ge a,\ B(t) \le b) = \mathbb{P}(B(t) \ge 2a - b)$ and $\mathbb{P}(M(t) \ge a) = \mathbb{P}(|B(t)| \ge a)$.

hypotheses.text: $B$ is a standard [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with $B(0) = 0$.
$T$ is a [stopping time](c:stopping-time) for the right-continuous [filtration](c:filtration) of $B$, with values in $[0, \infty]$.
For the law of the maximum, $d = 1$, $t > 0$, $a > 0$ and $b \le a$.

conclusion: $B^*$ is a standard Brownian motion, and for $d = 1$: $\mathbb{P}(M(t) \ge a,\ B(t) \le b) = \mathbb{P}(B(t) \ge 2a - b)$ and $\mathbb{P}(M(t) \ge a) = 2\mathbb{P}(B(t) \ge a) = \mathbb{P}(|B(t)| \ge a)$.

proofs.name: Strong Markov property and concatenation
proofs.slogan: After a stopping time the future increments form a fresh Brownian motion, and flipping it does not change the law of the glued path.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem: part (a) in every dimension and for every stopping time, and part (b) for linear Brownian motion.

roles.why: The strong Markov property and the symmetry of the centred [normal distribution](c:normal-distribution) are properties of Brownian motion.
The strong Markov property needs a stopping time. At other random times the reflected path is not Brownian.
The maximum and the level $2a - b$ need an order on the real line, and $t > 0$ makes $B(t)$ free of atoms.

steps.slogan: Write the path and its reflection as one measurable gluing of the stopped path and the future increments.
steps.detail: With $W(s) = B(T+s) - B(T)$ and the [continuous](c:continuous-function) map $\Psi(f, r, g)(t) = f(t) + g((t-r)^+)$, we get $B = \Psi(B^T, T, W)$ and $B^* = \Psi(B^T, T, -W)$ for bounded $T$.

steps.slogan: Use the strong Markov property to make the flipped and unflipped triples equal in law.
steps.detail: For bounded $T$, $W$ is a Brownian motion [independent](c:independence) of $\mathcal{F}^+(T)$, and $-W$ has the same law, so $(B^T, T, W)$ and $(B^T, T, -W)$ have the same law and $B^* \overset{d}{=} B$.

steps.slogan: Pass from bounded stopping times $T \wedge n$ to a general stopping time $T$.
steps.detail: For each $t$ the reflection at $T \wedge n$ equals $B^*(t)$ once $n$ is large, so every [finite-dimensional distribution](c:finite-dimensional-distribution) of $B^*$ is that of Brownian motion. With continuity this proves part (a).

steps.slogan: Identify the event of a high maximum and a low end point with one reflected event.
steps.detail: For the hitting time $\tau$ of level $a$, $M(t) \ge a$ if and only if $\tau \le t$, and then $B^*(t) = 2a - B(t)$. This gives the exact identity $\{M(t) \ge a,\ B(t) \le b\} = \{B^*(t) \ge 2a - b\}$.

steps.slogan: Read off the joint law and the law of the maximum from the normal law.
steps.detail: Part (a) gives $\mathbb{P}(B^*(t) \ge 2a - b) = \mathbb{P}(B(t) \ge 2a - b)$. Splitting on $B(t) > a$ and using that the [normal distribution](c:normal-distribution) has no atoms and is symmetric gives $\mathbb{P}(M(t) \ge a) = 2\mathbb{P}(B(t) \ge a) = \mathbb{P}(|B(t)| \ge a)$.

concepts.c:brownian-motion: Brownian motion is the process that the reflection keeps invariant in law.
concepts.c:stopping-time: The reflection time must be a stopping time for the strong Markov property.
concepts.c:filtration: The right-continuous filtration defines which random times are stopping times.
concepts.c:normal-distribution: The centred normal law of B(t) is symmetric and has no atoms.
concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity of the gluing map makes the reflected path a measurable function of its pieces.

statement: For [independent identically distributed](c:iid-random-variables) $X_1, X_2, \dots$ and a measurable set $B$ of sequences that is invariant under every finite [permutation](c:permutation) of coordinates, $\mathbb{P}((X_1, X_2, \dots) \in B)$ is $0$ or $1$.

hypotheses.text: The random elements $X_1, X_2, \dots$ of a measurable space $(S, \mathcal{S})$ are [independent identically distributed](c:iid-random-variables) with law $\mu$.

The set $B \in \mathcal{S}^{\otimes \mathbb{N}}$ satisfies $T_\pi^{-1}(B) = B$ for every finite [permutation](c:permutation) $\pi$, where $T_\pi(s) = (s_{\pi(1)}, s_{\pi(2)}, \dots)$. Such sets give the [exchangeable](c:exchangeability) events.

conclusion: $\mathbb{P}((X_1, X_2, \dots) \in B) \in \{0, 1\}$.

proofs.name: Approximation and block swap
proofs.slogan: Approximate the event by a cylinder event, swap two coordinate blocks, and show the event is independent of itself.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for i.i.d. random elements of an arbitrary measurable space.

roles.why: Independence makes the law a [product measure](c:product-measure), which is invariant under coordinate permutations and makes disjoint blocks independent.
Invariance of $B$ under the block swap turns the approximation by the first block into an approximation by the second block.

steps.slogan: Identify the law of the sequence with an invariant [product measure](c:product-measure).
steps.detail: The law $Q$ of $(X_1, X_2, \dots)$ agrees with $\mu^{\otimes \mathbb{N}}$ on cylinder sets, which form a [π-system](c:pi-system), so $Q = \mu^{\otimes \mathbb{N}}$. The same argument shows $Q \circ T_\pi^{-1} = Q$ for every finite permutation $\pi$.

steps.slogan: Approximate the set $B$ by cylinder sets on finitely many coordinates.
steps.detail: The sets that cylinder sets approximate in $Q$-measure form a [Dynkin system](c:dynkin-system) that contains the algebra of cylinder sets. So there are $B_j = \{(s_1, \dots, s_{n_j}) \in C_j\}$ with $Q(B \,\Delta\, B_j) \to 0$.

steps.slogan: Swap the first two coordinate blocks to move the approximating set to fresh coordinates.
steps.detail: With $\pi$ exchanging $i$ and $i + n$ for $i \le n$, the set $B'_j = T_\pi^{-1}(B_j)$ depends on coordinates $n+1, \dots, 2n$. Since $T_\pi^{-1}(B) = B$ and $Q$ is invariant, $Q(B \,\Delta\, B'_j) = Q(B \,\Delta\, B_j) \to 0$.

steps.slogan: Compute the probability of the intersection of the two independent block events.
steps.detail: Disjoint coordinate blocks are independent under the product measure, so $Q(B_j \cap B'_j) = Q(B_j)^2$. Both $B_j$ and $B'_j$ approach $B$, so $Q(B_j \cap B'_j) \to Q(B)$ and $Q(B_j) \to Q(B)$.

steps.slogan: Solve the equation $p = p^2$ for the probability of the permutable event.
steps.detail: Passing to the limit gives $p = p^2$ for $p = Q(B)$, so the event is independent of itself and its probability is $0$ or $1$.

statement: If $\mu_N$ is a symmetric probability measure on $\Omega^N$ and $\tilde\mu_N = \int \bar\rho_Z^{\otimes N}\, \mu_N(dZ)$ is the [mixture](c:mixture-of-distributions) of i.i.d. laws drawn from the [empirical measure](c:empirical-measure) $\bar\rho_Z$, then for $1 \le n \le N$ the $n$-marginals satisfy $\sup_A |\mu_N^{(n)}(A) - \tilde\mu_N^{(n)}(A)| \le 1 - \frac{N(N-1)\cdots(N-n+1)}{N^n} \le \frac{n(n-1)}{2N}$.

hypotheses.text: $\mu_N$ is a probability measure on $\Omega^N$ that is invariant under every [permutation](c:permutation) of the coordinates, that is, it is the law of an [exchangeable](c:exchangeability) vector.
The marginal size satisfies $1 \le n \le N$.

conclusion: $\sup_A |\mu_N^{(n)}(A) - \tilde\mu_N^{(n)}(A)| \le 1 - \frac{N(N-1)\cdots(N-n+1)}{N^n} \le \frac{n(n-1)}{2N}$, so the [total variation distance](c:total-variation-distance) $\int d|\mu_N^{(n)} - \tilde\mu_N^{(n)}|$ is at most $n(n-1)/N$.

proofs.name: Expansion of the empirical tensor power
proofs.slogan: Expand the tensor power of the empirical measure: injective index maps give the true marginal by symmetry, and the rest is a small positive remainder.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for an arbitrary measurable space and all $1 \le n \le N$.

roles.why: Symmetry makes every injective selection of $n$ coordinates have the law of the first $n$ coordinates.
For $n \le N$ injective maps exist and each factor $1 - (j-1)/N$ lies in $(0, 1]$.

steps.slogan: Expand the $n$-th tensor power of the [empirical measure](c:empirical-measure) as a sum over index maps.
steps.detail: Multiplying out the sums gives $\bar\rho_Z^{\otimes n} = N^{-n}\sum_{\gamma} \delta_{(z_{\gamma(1)}, \dots, z_{\gamma(n)})}$ over all $N^n$ maps $\gamma : \{1..n\} \to \{1..N\}$, which is sampling $n$ times with replacement.

steps.slogan: Show that each injective index map reproduces the true marginal of $\mu_N$.
steps.detail: An injective $\gamma$ extends to a [permutation](c:permutation) $\sigma$ of all coordinates, and symmetry of $\mu_N$ gives $\int 1_A(Z_\gamma)\,d\mu_N = \mu_N^{(n)}(A)$. There are $N(N-1)\cdots(N-n+1)$ such maps.

steps.slogan: Write the mixture marginal as a multiple of the true marginal plus a positive remainder.
steps.detail:
With $c = N(N-1)\cdots(N-n+1)/N^n$ we get $	ilde\mu_N^{(n)} = c\,\mu_N^{(n)} + 
u$ for a positive measure $
u$ of mass $1-c$. The difference $(1-c)\mu_N^{(n)}(A) - 
u(A)$ lies in $[-(1-c), 1-c]$.

steps.slogan: Bound one minus the product of the factors by the sum of their defects.
steps.detail: By induction, $\prod_j (1 - a_j) \ge 1 - \sum_j a_j$ for $a_j \in [0,1]$. With $a_j = (j-1)/N$ this gives $1 - c \le n(n-1)/(2N)$, which completes the bound.

new_concepts.name: empirical measure
new_concepts.reminder: The empirical measure of a sample puts mass $1/n$ at each of the $n$ sample points.
new_concepts.definition: For random variables $X_1,\dots,X_n$ with values in a measurable space $S$, the empirical measure is the random [probability measure](c:probability-measure) $\mu_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{X_i}$, where $\delta_x$ is the [Dirac measure](c:dirac-measure) at $x$. So $\mu_n(A)$ is the fraction of the sample points that lie in $A$. If the $X_i$ are [iid](c:iid-random-variables) with law $\mu$ on a Polish space, then $\mu_n\to\mu$ weakly almost surely.

statement: Let $(\rho^{(n)})_{n \ge 1}$ be [density matrices](c:density-matrix) on $(\mathbb{C}^d)^{\otimes n}$ that are invariant under every [permutation](c:permutation) of the factors and consistent under the [partial trace](c:partial-trace). Then $\rho^{(n)} = \int \sigma^{\otimes n}\, m(d\sigma)$ for all $n$, for a unique probability measure $m$ on the density matrices of $\mathbb{C}^d$. This is a [mixture](c:mixture-of-distributions) of [tensor](c:tensor-product) powers. If $\rho^{(2)}$ is bosonic, $m$ is carried by [pure states](c:pure-state).

hypotheses.text: The one-particle space $\mathbb{C}^d$ has finite dimension $d$.
Each $\rho^{(n)}$ is a [density matrix](c:density-matrix) on $(\mathbb{C}^d)^{\otimes n}$ with $U_\pi \rho^{(n)} U_\pi^* = \rho^{(n)}$ for every [permutation](c:permutation) $\pi$.
The [partial trace](c:partial-trace) over the last factor gives $\mathrm{Tr}_{n+1}\rho^{(n+1)} = \rho^{(n)}$ for all $n$.

conclusion: There is a unique probability measure $m$ on the density matrices of $\mathbb{C}^d$ with $\rho^{(n)} = \int \sigma^{\otimes n}\, m(d\sigma)$ for all $n \ge 1$, and $m$ is carried by pure states when $\rho^{(2)}$ lives on the symmetric subspace.

proofs.name: Reduction to the classical theorem by an informationally complete measurement
proofs.slogan: Measure every system with the same informationally complete measurement, apply classical de Finetti to the outcomes, and show that the mixing measure sees only physical states.
proofs.scope: Outline of the published proof of Caves, Fuchs and Schack, Section IV, with the uniqueness and the bosonic clause added.

roles.why: A measurement with $d^2$ linearly independent outcomes exists only in finite dimension, and its outcome products form a basis.
Permutation invariance of $\rho^{(N)}$ makes the outcome probabilities [exchangeable](c:exchangeability).
Consistency makes the outcome laws for different $N$ fit together into one infinite exchangeable sequence.

steps.slogan: Build a measurement with $d^2$ linearly independent positive outcomes that sum to the identity.
steps.detail: Take $d^2$ rank-one projections that span all $d \times d$ matrices and set $E_\alpha = G^{-1/2}\Pi_\alpha G^{-1/2}$ with $G = \sum_\alpha \Pi_\alpha$. This is a [POVM](c:positive-operator-valued-measure) whose elements are a basis.

steps.slogan: The outcomes of the same measurement on every system form an exchangeable sequence.
steps.detail: The numbers $\mathrm{Tr}[\rho^{(N)} E_{\alpha_1} \otimes \cdots \otimes E_{\alpha_N}]$ are symmetric and consistent probabilities. The classical de Finetti theorem writes them as $\int p_{\alpha_1} \cdots p_{\alpha_N} P(dp)$ for a unique measure $P$ on the [simplex](c:simplex).

steps.slogan: Turn each probability vector into a Hermitian operator of trace one and lift the identity.
steps.detail: Let $A_p$ solve $\mathrm{Tr}(A_p E_\alpha) = p_\alpha$. The products $E_{\alpha_1} \otimes \cdots \otimes E_{\alpha_N}$ are a [basis](c:basis), so $\rho^{(N)} = \int A_p^{\otimes N} P(dp)$.

steps.slogan: Even tensor powers of an unphysical operator give probabilities above one, so they get no weight.
steps.detail: If $A_q$ has an [eigenvalue](c:eigenvalue) $-\lambda < 0$ with eigenvector $\psi$, then $\Pi = 1 - |\psi\rangle\langle\psi|$ gives $1 \ge \mathrm{Tr}[\rho^{(N)}\Pi^{\otimes N}] \ge (1+\lambda/2)^N P(B)$ near $q$ for even $N$. So $P(B) = 0$, and a countable cover finishes.

steps.slogan: Move the measure to density matrices, prove uniqueness, and treat bosonic states with the swap operator.
steps.detail: The image $m$ of $P$ under $p \mapsto A_p$ represents every $\rho^{(n)}$. Any other representing measure has the same image on the simplex by classical uniqueness. For bosonic $\rho^{(2)}$, $\int (1 - \mathrm{Tr}\,\sigma^2)\, m(d\sigma) = 0$ forces pure states.

statement: For a bosonic [density matrix](c:density-matrix) $\Gamma_N$ on the [symmetric subspace](c:symmetric-subspace) of $(\mathbb{C}^d)^{\otimes N}$, the measure $\mu_N(du) = \dim \mathrm{Sym}^N \langle u^{\otimes N}, \Gamma_N u^{\otimes N}\rangle du$ on [pure states](c:pure-state) satisfies $\mathrm{Tr}\,|\gamma^{(k)} - \int |u^{\otimes k}\rangle\langle u^{\otimes k}|\,d\mu_N| \le 4kd/N$. A [permutation](c:permutation)-invariant state $\xi_N$ on $(\mathbb{C}^d)^{\otimes N}$ has $\mathrm{Tr}\,|\xi^{(k)} - \int \sigma^{\otimes k}\,dm(\sigma)| \le 4kd^2/N$ for some probability measure $m$.

hypotheses.text: The one-particle space $H = \mathbb{C}^d$ has finite dimension $d$.

$\Gamma_N$ is a [density matrix](c:density-matrix) on the [symmetric subspace](c:symmetric-subspace) $\mathrm{Sym}^N(H)$, or $\xi_N$ is a density matrix on $H^{\otimes N}$ that commutes with every [permutation](c:permutation) of the factors.
The number $k$ of kept particles satisfies $1 \le k \le N$, and $\gamma^{(k)}$ is the [partial trace](c:partial-trace) over the other $N - k$ particles.

conclusion: $\mathrm{Tr}\,|\gamma^{(k)} - \int |u^{\otimes k}\rangle\langle u^{\otimes k}|\,\mu_N(du)| \le \min\{2kd/(N-kd), 4kd/N\}$ (the first bound for $N > kd$), and $\mathrm{Tr}\,|\xi^{(k)} - \int \sigma^{\otimes k}\,m(d\sigma)| \le 4kd^2/N$.

proofs.name: Lower symbol in coherent states and symmetric purification
proofs.slogan: Use the coherent-state lower symbol as the de Finetti measure, bound the error by a dimension ratio, and purify general states into bosonic ones.
proofs.scope: Outline of the published proofs: Lewin, Nam and Rougerie, Section 3, for bosonic states, and Christandl, König, Mitchison and Renner, Lemma II.5 and Theorem II.7, for permutation-invariant states.

roles.why: The uniform measure on the [unit sphere](c:unit-sphere) and Schur's formula exist only in finite dimension, and the bound depends on $d$.
Bosonic symmetry puts $\Psi$ in the space where Schur's formula holds. Permutation invariance makes the purification bosonic.
The kept $k$ particles and the traced $N-k$ particles give the two Schur formulas whose dimensions are compared.

steps.slogan: Resolve the identity on the symmetric subspace with coherent product states $u^{\otimes N}$.
steps.detail: The [unitary group](c:unitary-group) acts [irreducibly](c:irreducible-representation) on $\mathrm{Sym}^N(\mathbb{C}^d)$, so Schur's lemma gives $\dim \mathrm{Sym}^N \int |u^{\otimes N}\rangle\langle u^{\otimes N}|\,du = 1$. This makes $\mu_N$ a probability measure.

steps.slogan: Write the error as an integral and split it into two terms of the same size.
steps.detail: For a bounded $A$, $\mathrm{Tr}[A(\gamma^{(k)} - \tilde\gamma^{(k)})] = \dim \mathrm{Sym}^N \int \langle \Psi, P_u^{\otimes N}(A \otimes 1)(1 - P_u^{\otimes N})\Psi\rangle du$. The identity $PA(1-P) = A(1-P) - (1-P)A(1-P)$ and Schur's formula bound each part by $\|A\|(\dim \mathrm{Sym}^N/\dim \mathrm{Sym}^{N-k} - 1)$.

steps.slogan: Bound the ratio of the symmetric-subspace dimensions by Bernoulli's inequality.
steps.detail: Duality between the trace norm and the operator norm gives the error $2(\dim \mathrm{Sym}^N/\dim \mathrm{Sym}^{N-k} - 1)$, and $\dim \mathrm{Sym}^{N-k}/\dim \mathrm{Sym}^N \ge 1 - dk/N$ gives $2kd/(N-kd) \le 4kd/N$.

steps.slogan: Purify a permutation-invariant state into a bosonic state of doubled local dimension.
steps.detail: The vector $(1 \otimes \sqrt{\xi_N})(\sum_i e_i \otimes e_i)^{\otimes N}$ is symmetric in the pairs and has $\xi_N$ as its [partial trace](c:partial-trace). The bosonic bound with dimension $d^2$, followed by the partial trace over the copies, gives $4kd^2/N$.

new_concepts.name: symmetric subspace
new_concepts.reminder: The subspace of a tensor power of vectors that every permutation of the factors leaves unchanged.
new_concepts.definition: For a Hilbert space $H$, the symmetric subspace $\mathrm{Sym}^N(H) \subset H^{\otimes N}$ is the set of vectors $\Psi$ with $U_\pi \Psi = \Psi$ for every [permutation](c:permutation) $\pi$ of the $N$ [tensor](c:tensor-product) factors. It is the state space of $N$ bosons, and $\dim \mathrm{Sym}^N(\mathbb{C}^d) = \binom{N+d-1}{d-1}$.

statement: Let $(X_{st})$ be a jointly [exchangeable array](c:exchangeable-array) with $X_{st} = X_{ts}$, that is a random colouring of the edges of the complete [graph](c:graph) on $\mathbb{N}$ with colours in a [standard Borel space](c:standard-borel-space) $K$. Then there is a measurable $f : [0,1]^4 \to K$, symmetric in its two middle arguments, such that $(X_{st})$ has the same law as $(f(\xi_\emptyset, \xi_s, \xi_t, \xi_{st}))$ for independent [uniform](c:uniform-distribution) variables $\xi$ on $[0,1]$.

hypotheses.text: The vertex set $S$ is countably infinite.
The colour space $K$ is a [standard Borel space](c:standard-borel-space).
The law of $(X_{st})$ does not change under a [permutation](c:permutation) of $S$ that moves finitely many points and acts on both indices.

conclusion: There is a measurable $f$ with $f(\alpha, x, y, u) = f(\alpha, y, x, u)$ such that $(X_{st}) \overset{d}{=} (f(\xi_\emptyset, \xi_s, \xi_t, \xi_{st}))$ for independent uniform $\xi_\emptyset$, $\xi_s$ and $\xi_{st}$.

proofs.name: Reference vertices and noise outsourcing
proofs.slogan: Use half of the vertices as references, prove conditional independence of the edges, then code every kernel by uniform noise.
proofs.scope: Outline of the proof of Corollary 3.5 and of the transfer by Lemma 4.2 in Austin, Probability Surveys 5 (2008), pp. 100-104 and p. 127.

roles.why: An infinite vertex set splits into two infinite halves, so the second half supplies reference vertices for every finite configuration.
Noise outsourcing needs a standard Borel target to write each probability kernel as a measurable function of a uniform variable.
Permutations that move vertices into the reference half keep the law, and this drives every step of the argument.

steps.slogan: Split the vertices into two infinite halves and keep the second half as reference vertices.
steps.detail: By [exchangeability](c:exchangeability) the induced graph on the first half $S_1$ has the same law as the whole graph, so it is enough to represent the edges inside $S_1$.

steps.slogan: Each vertex of the first half gets a type from its edges to the reference half.
steps.detail: The type $Y_s$ lists the colours of the edges from $s$ to $S_2$ and of the edges inside $S_2$. Permutations of $S_1$ permute the types, so $(Y_s)$ is an exchangeable sequence.

steps.slogan: Fewer reference vertices give the same conditional expectation of an edge colour.
steps.detail: Shrinking the reference set applies an [orthogonal projection](c:orthogonal-projection) to the [conditional expectation](c:conditional-expectation) of $\varphi(X_{st})$. Exchangeability shows that the $L^2$ norm does not change, so the two conditional expectations are equal.

steps.slogan: Given all types, the edge colours are independent with one symmetric kernel.
steps.detail: Moving the other vertices of each edge into the reference half proves [conditional independence](c:conditional-independence) of the edges given the types. The conditional law of $X_{st}$ is $P_2(Y_s, Y_t, \cdot)$ for one symmetric [kernel](c:markov-kernel) $P_2$.

steps.slogan: De Finetti's theorem and noise outsourcing turn the kernels into one function of uniform variables.
steps.detail:
De Finetti's theorem gives a random law $
u$ such that the types are i.i.d. with law $
u$. Noise outsourcing writes $
u$, the types and the edge colours as functions of independent [uniform](c:uniform-distribution) variables, and this defines $f$.

new_concepts.name: exchangeable array
new_concepts.reminder: An exchangeable array is a random matrix whose law does not change when you permute its rows and columns.
new_concepts.definition: An array $(X_{ij})_{i,j\in\mathbb{N}}$ of [random variables](c:random-variable) is jointly exchangeable when $(X_{\sigma(i)\sigma(j)})$ has the same [joint distribution](c:joint-distribution) as $(X_{ij})$ for every finite [permutation](c:permutation) $\sigma$ of $\mathbb{N}$. It is separately exchangeable when $(X_{\sigma(i)\tau(j)})$ has the law of $(X_{ij})$ for all finite permutations $\sigma$ and $\tau$. The Aldous–Hoover theorem represents a separately exchangeable array as $X_{ij}=f(U,U_i,V_j,U_{ij})$ with iid uniform variables $U,U_i,V_j,U_{ij}$, and it gives a similar formula in the joint case.

statement: Let $\Pi$ be an [exchangeable random partition](c:exchangeable-random-partition) of $\mathbb{N}$. Then the ranked block proportions $P^{\downarrow}_i = \lim_n N^{\downarrow}_{n,i}/n$ exist [almost surely](c:almost-sure-convergence). Given $P^{\downarrow} = p$, $\Pi$ is the paintbox partition: [uniform](c:uniform-distribution) points $U_i$ share a block when they fall in the same interval of length $p_k$. So the law of $\Pi$ is a [mixture](c:mixture-of-distributions) of paintbox laws.

hypotheses.text: $\Pi$ is a random [partition](c:set-partition) of the infinite set $\mathbb{N}$, so its restrictions $\Pi_n$ to $\{1, \dots, n\}$ are consistent.
The law of $\Pi$ is invariant under every permutation of $\mathbb{N}$ that moves finitely many points.

conclusion: $N^{\downarrow}_{n,i}/n \to P^{\downarrow}_i$ almost surely for each $i$, and conditionally on $P^{\downarrow} = p$ the partition $\Pi$ has the paintbox law of $p$.

proofs.name: Uniform marks and de Finetti's theorem
proofs.slogan: Label each block with an independent uniform mark, apply de Finetti to the marks, and read the partition from the atoms.
proofs.scope: Outline of the proof sketch in Pitman, Combinatorial Stochastic Processes, pp. 44-45, after Aldous (1985), p. 88.

roles.why: De Finetti's theorem needs an infinite exchangeable sequence of marks, one mark for each integer.
Exchangeability of the partition makes the sequence of marks [exchangeable](c:exchangeability).

steps.slogan: Give each block an independent uniform mark and copy the mark to its elements.
steps.detail: With i.i.d. uniform $U_j$ independent of $\Pi$, put $X_n = U_j$ when $n$ lies in the $j$-th block. Then $X_m = X_n$ exactly when $m$ and $n$ share a block, and a relabelling argument shows that $(X_n)$ is exchangeable.

steps.slogan: De Finetti's theorem gives a random directing distribution for the marks.
steps.detail: Conditionally on a random distribution $F$ the marks are i.i.d. $F$, and the [empirical distribution](c:empirical-distribution) functions converge to $F$ uniformly almost surely by Glivenko–Cantelli.

steps.slogan: Ties among the marks occur only at atoms, which gives the paintbox law.
steps.detail: Two i.i.d. draws from $F$ coincide only at an [atom](c:atom), so given $F$ the partition is the paintbox of the ranked atom sizes of $F$. The continuous part of $F$ produces singletons.

steps.slogan: Block proportions are the jumps of the empirical distribution, so they converge to the atom sizes.
steps.detail: The $i$-th largest jump of $F_n$ is $N^{\downarrow}_{n,i}/n$. Jumps differ by at most twice the uniform distance, and ranking is 1-Lipschitz, so $N^{\downarrow}_{n,i}/n \to P^{\downarrow}_i$ almost surely.

new_concepts.name: exchangeable random partition
new_concepts.reminder: An exchangeable random partition of $\mathbb{N}$ has a law that does not change when you relabel finitely many integers.
new_concepts.definition: A random partition $\Pi$ of $\mathbb{N}=\{1,2,\dots\}$ is a random variable with values in the [set partitions](c:set-partition) of $\mathbb{N}$, measurable for the sigma-algebra that the restrictions of $\Pi$ to $\{1,\dots,n\}$ generate. It is exchangeable when, for every [permutation](c:permutation) $\sigma$ of $\mathbb{N}$ that moves only finitely many points, the relabeled partition $\sigma(\Pi)$, with blocks $\sigma(B)$ for the blocks $B$ of $\Pi$, has the same law as $\Pi$. By Kingman's theorem, every such $\Pi$ is a mixture of paintbox partitions.

statement: Let $(X_n)_{n \ge 1}$ be an infinite sequence of random variables in a [standard Borel space](c:standard-borel-space). If every [subsequence](c:subsequence) $(X_{n_1}, X_{n_2}, \dots)$ with $n_1 < n_2 < \cdots$ has the same law as $(X_n)$, then $(X_n)$ is [exchangeable](c:exchangeability). In fact the $X_n$ are [conditionally independent](c:conditional-independence) and [identically distributed](c:ident-distrib) given the [tail σ-algebra](c:tail-sigma-algebra).

hypotheses.text: The sequence $(X_n)_{n \ge 1}$ is infinite, with values in a [standard Borel space](c:standard-borel-space).
Every [subsequence](c:subsequence) $(X_{n_1}, X_{n_2}, \dots)$ with $n_1 < n_2 < \cdots$ has the same law as $(X_n)$.

conclusion: $(X_n)$ is exchangeable, and $P(X_1 \in B_1, \dots, X_k \in B_k \mid \mathcal{T}) = \prod_{i \le k} P(X_1 \in B_i \mid \mathcal{T})$ for the tail σ-algebra $\mathcal{T}$.

proofs.name: Projection squeeze and martingale convergence
proofs.slogan: Conditional expectations with equal laws and nested σ-algebras are equal, and this gives independence given the tail.
proofs.scope: Outline of the proof of Theorem 6.1, property (A), in Aldous, Exchangeability and related topics (1985), pp. 42-45, through Lemma 6.3, Proposition 6.4 and Lemma 6.5.

roles.why: An infinite sequence has far blocks $(X_m, X_{m+1}, \dots)$ for every $m$, and the tail σ-algebra is their limit.
Spreadability moves the conditioning block far away and moves $X_n$ to the front without a change of law.

steps.slogan: A conditional expectation with the norm of a finer one is equal to it.
steps.detail: If $\mathcal F \subset \mathcal G$, then $E[Y \mid \mathcal F]$ is the [orthogonal projection](c:orthogonal-projection) of $E[Y \mid \mathcal G]$. Equal $L^2$ norms force equality, and [martingale](c:martingale) convergence carries the norms to the limit.

steps.slogan: Spreadability lets the first variable see a far block instead of its neighbours.
steps.detail: The vectors $(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n)$ and $(X_1, X_m, \dots, X_{m+n-2})$ have the same law. So the [conditional expectations](c:conditional-expectation) of $\varphi(X_1)$ given the other entries have the same law, and the squeeze makes them equal.

steps.slogan: Letting the far block move to infinity gives independence given the tail.
steps.detail: Backward martingale convergence gives $E[\varphi(X_1) \mid X_2, X_3, \dots] = E[\varphi(X_1) \mid \mathcal T]$. The same holds for every shifted sequence, so the $X_n$ are [conditionally independent](c:conditional-independence) given $\mathcal T$.

steps.slogan: Moving a later variable to the front shows that all conditional laws agree.
steps.detail: The sequences $(X_1, X_{n+1}, \dots)$ and $(X_n, X_{n+1}, \dots)$ have the same law, so $E[\varphi(X_n) \mid \mathcal T] = E[\varphi(X_1) \mid \mathcal T]$. Conditionally i.i.d. variables are [exchangeable](c:exchangeability).

statement:
A probability law on $\mathbb{R}$ is [infinitely divisible](c:infinitely-divisible-distribution) if and only if its [characteristic function](c:characteristic-function) is $\varphi(t) = \exp ig(ict - \sigma^2 t^2/2 + \int (e^{itx} - 1 - 	frac{itx}{1+x^2})\,
u(dx) ig)$ with $c \in \mathbb{R}$, $\sigma^2 \ge 0$ and a [Lévy measure](c:levy-measure) $
u$. The triple $(c, \sigma^2, 
u)$ is unique.

hypotheses.text: The law is a probability measure on $\mathbb{R}$, and [infinite divisibility](c:infinitely-divisible-distribution) means that it is the $n$-fold [convolution](c:convolution) power of a probability measure for every $n$.
In the formula $c \in \mathbb{R}$, $\sigma^2 \ge 0$, and $\nu$ is a measure on $\mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}$ with $\int x^2/(1+x^2)\,\nu(dx) < \infty$.

conclusion: The [infinitely divisible](c:infinitely-divisible-distribution) laws are exactly the laws whose [characteristic function](c:characteristic-function) has the Lévy–Khintchine form, and the form determines the triple $(c, \sigma^2, \nu)$.

proofs.name: Through a Lévy process and its decomposition
proofs.slogan: Embed the law in a Lévy process, read its exponent off the Lévy–Itô decomposition, and recover the triple by averaging.
proofs.scope: The full equivalence and the uniqueness in dimension one. The necessity part rests on the cited Lévy–Itô decomposition.

roles.why: Infinite divisibility gives roots of every order, which keep the characteristic function away from zero and give all real powers $e^{-s\psi}$.
The integrability of $\nu$ makes the exponent finite and justifies dominated convergence in the limits and in the uniqueness argument.

steps.slogan: Compound Poisson laws approximate every formula, so each formula is an infinitely divisible characteristic function.
steps.detail: Truncating $\nu$ to $|x| \ge \varepsilon$ gives a [compound Poisson](c:compound-poisson-process) law times a normal law. Dominated convergence and Lévy's continuity theorem pass to $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, and the triple divided by $n$ gives the $n$-th root.

steps.slogan: Roots of every order keep the characteristic function away from zero.
steps.detail: The functions $|\varphi|^{2/n}$ are characteristic functions and tend to the indicator of $\{\varphi \ne 0\}$. That limit is continuous at 0, so it is a continuous characteristic function, and it must be identically 1.

steps.slogan: A continuous logarithm gives the real powers $e^{-s\psi}$ as characteristic functions.
steps.detail: Write $\varphi = e^{-\psi}$ with $\psi$ continuous and $\psi(0) = 0$. The $n$-th roots equal $e^{-\psi/n}$, so $e^{-q\psi}$ is a characteristic function for rational $q \ge 0$, and limits give every real $s \ge 0$.

steps.slogan: Build a Lévy process whose value at time one has the given law.
steps.detail: Each $e^{-s\psi}$ is a [positive-definite function](c:positive-definite-function), so Bochner's theorem and Kolmogorov's extension theorem give a [Lévy process](c:levy-process) with $E[e^{iuX_s}] = e^{-s\psi(u)}$.

steps.slogan: Read the exponent off the independent pieces of the Lévy–Itô decomposition.
steps.detail: The Gaussian part, the drift, the compound Poisson big jumps and the compensated small jumps are independent, so their characteristic functions multiply. A change of compensator gives Durrett's form with $c = \gamma + \int x(\frac{1}{1+x^2} - 1(|x|<1))\,\nu(dx)$.

steps.slogan: Growth at infinity gives the variance, and averaging over shifts recovers the Lévy measure.
steps.detail: $\sigma^2 = \lim 2\psi(s)/s^2$. The averaged difference $h(u) - \frac12\int_{-1}^{1} h(u+v)\,dv$ is minus the Fourier transform of the finite measure $(1 - \sin x/x)\,\nu(dx)$, which determines $\nu$, and then $c$.

new_concepts.name: compound Poisson process
new_concepts.reminder: A compound Poisson process adds up iid random jumps at the arrival times of a Poisson process.
new_concepts.definition: Let $(N_t)_{t\ge0}$ be a [Poisson process](c:poisson-process) with rate $\lambda>0$, and let $Y_1,Y_2,\dots$ be [iid random variables](c:iid-random-variables) that are independent of $(N_t)$. The compound Poisson process is $S_t=\sum_{i=1}^{N_t}Y_i$, with $S_t=0$ when $N_t=0$. It has independent and stationary increments, and $E[e^{i\theta S_t}]=\exp(\lambda t(\varphi_Y(\theta)-1))$, where $\varphi_Y$ is the [characteristic function](c:characteristic-function) of $Y_1$.

new_concepts.name: infinitely divisible distribution
new_concepts.reminder: An infinitely divisible law is, for every $n$, the law of a sum of $n$ iid random variables.
new_concepts.definition: A [probability distribution](c:probability-distribution) $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$ is infinitely divisible when for every $n\ge1$ there is a probability distribution $\mu_n$ with $\mu=\mu_n^{*n}$, the $n$-fold [convolution](c:convolution) power. Equivalently, for every $n$, a random variable with law $\mu$ has the law of $Y_{n,1}+\dots+Y_{n,n}$ with [iid random variables](c:iid-random-variables) $Y_{n,k}$. The Lévy–Khintchine formula describes all such laws by a drift, a Gaussian covariance and a [Lévy measure](c:levy-measure).

new_concepts.name: Levy measure
new_concepts.reminder: The Lévy measure $\nu(A)$ is the expected number of jumps per unit time of a Lévy process with size in $A$.
new_concepts.definition:
A Lévy measure on $\mathbb{R}^d$ is a [measure](c:measure) $
u$ on $\mathbb{R}^d\setminus\{0\}$ with $\int\min(1,|x|^2)\,
u(dx)<\infty$. In the Lévy–Khintchine formula for an [infinitely divisible distribution](c:infinitely-divisible-distribution) or a [Lévy process](c:levy-process) $X$, it describes the jumps: $
u(A)=\mathbb{E}[\#\{s\le1:\Delta X_s\in A\}]$ for each Borel set $A$ at positive distance from $0$. It can have infinite total mass near $0$, which means infinitely many small jumps.

new_concepts.name: Levy process
new_concepts.reminder: A Lévy process starts at zero and has stationary independent increments and right-continuous paths with left limits.
new_concepts.definition: A Lévy process is a [stochastic process](c:stochastic-process) $(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ with values in $\mathbb{R}^d$ such that $X_0=0$ almost surely, $X$ has [independent increments](c:independent-increments), the law of $X_{t+s}-X_s$ depends only on $t$, and almost every path is [càdlàg](c:is-cadlag). Each $X_t$ has an [infinitely divisible distribution](c:infinitely-divisible-distribution), and the Lévy–Khintchine formula gives $\mathbb{E}[e^{i\langle u,X_t\rangle}]=e^{t\psi(u)}$ with an exponent $\psi$ that a drift, a Gaussian covariance and a [Lévy measure](c:levy-measure) determine.

statement: Let $X$ be a [Lévy process](c:levy-process) in $\mathbb{R}^n$ with càdlàg paths, and let $N_t(A)$ count its jumps $\Delta X_s \in A$ for $s \le t$. Then $\nu(A) = E[N_1(A)]$ is a [Lévy measure](c:levy-measure), the counts on sets away from $0$ are [Poisson processes](c:poisson-process), and $X_t = B_t + \gamma t + \sum_{s \le t} \Delta X_s 1(|\Delta X_s| \ge 1) + X^d_t$. Here $B$ is a continuous centered [Gaussian process](c:gaussian-process) independent of the jumps, and $X^d_t$ is the $L^2$ limit of the compensated sums of the jumps with $\varepsilon \le |\Delta X_s| < 1$.

hypotheses.text: $X$ is a [Lévy process](c:levy-process): $X_0 = 0$, the increment $X_{t+s} - X_t$ is independent of the past and has the law of $X_s$, $X$ is continuous in probability, and its càdlàg version is used.

conclusion: Every [Lévy process](c:levy-process) is the sum of an independent continuous [Gaussian process](c:gaussian-process), a linear drift, a finite sum of big jumps and an $L^2$ limit of compensated small jumps, with jump counts given by [Poisson processes](c:poisson-process).

proofs.name: Square-integrable martingales and orthogonal jumps
proofs.slogan: Peel off the jumps shell by shell as orthogonal compensated martingales, and show that the continuous remainder is Gaussian.
proofs.scope: Outline of the proof of Theorem 3.12 (A) in Bretagnolle's notes (arXiv:1506.06624). The formula for the characteristic exponent and its uniqueness are not covered.

roles.why: Independent stationary increments give the strong Markov property, Poisson jump counts, exponential martingales and the independence of the pieces.

steps.slogan: Take càdlàg paths and get all moments when the jumps are bounded.
steps.detail: The exponential [martingales](c:martingale) $e^{i\langle u, X_t\rangle}/E[e^{i\langle u, X_t\rangle}]$ give a càdlàg version. With the strong Markov property, the times at which $X$ moves by $M$ have i.i.d. gaps, so $P(|X_t| \ge 2kM) \le e^t a^k$ with $a < 1$ when no jump reaches size $M$.

steps.slogan: Count the jumps in sets away from zero and remove the big jumps.
steps.detail: For $0 \notin \bar A$ the count $N_t(A)$ is a counting process with [independent increments](c:independent-increments) and unit jumps, so it is a [Poisson process](c:poisson-process). After the jumps with $|x| \ge 1$ are removed, the rest has all moments, mean $\gamma t$, and becomes a centered martingale $X''$.

steps.slogan: Compensated jump integrals satisfy an $L^2$ isometry and form closed martingale subspaces.
steps.detail:
For $0 
otin  ar B$, $E[(\int_B f\,dN_t - t\int_B f\,d
u)^2] = t\int_B f^2\,d
u$. Doob's inequality makes the space of square-integrable càdlàg martingales complete, and the compensated integrals form a closed subspace.

steps.slogan: Martingales without common jump times are orthogonal, so the jump pieces are independent.
steps.detail: Sums over fine partitions show that the product of two such exponential martingales has mean zero when one has finite variation. This factorizes the joint [characteristic function](c:characteristic-function), so jump processes on disjoint sets are independent.

steps.slogan: Sum the compensated shell jumps in $L^2$ and show that the remainder is continuous.
steps.detail: Orthogonality gives $t\int_{A_m} |x|^2\,\nu(dx) \le E|X''_t|^2$, so the compensated shell sums converge in $L^2$ to $X^d$. The remainder $X'' - Y(A_m)$ has no jump above $1/(m+1)$, so its uniform limit $X^c$ is continuous.

steps.slogan: A continuous centered Lévy process is Gaussian by a second-order Taylor expansion.
steps.detail: Along a fine partition, a second-order expansion gives $e^{-t\psi(u)} - 1 = -\frac{u^2}{2}\int_0^t e^{-s\psi(u)}\,ds$, because path continuity kills the remainder. So $\psi(u) = u^2/2$ after scaling, and the continuous part is a [Gaussian process](c:gaussian-process).

steps.slogan: Add the Gaussian part, the drift, the big jumps and the compensated small jumps.
steps.detail: The pieces give $X_t = X^c_t + \gamma t + X_t(\{|x| \ge 1\}) + X^d_t$. The continuous part is independent of all jumps by the orthogonality step, and the two bounds on $\nu$ make it a [Lévy measure](c:levy-measure).

concepts.c:levy-process: The theorem decomposes the paths of an arbitrary Lévy process.
concepts.c:levy-measure: The mean jump counts per unit time form the Lévy measure of the process.

concepts.c:independent-increments: Independent increments make the jump counts Poisson and the pieces independent.
concepts.c:characteristic-function: Factorized joint characteristic functions prove the independence of the pieces.

statement: A function $\varphi$ is the [characteristic function](c:characteristic-function) of a [stable distribution](c:stable-distribution) on $\mathbb{R}$ if and only if $\varphi(t) = \exp\big(i\mu t - |ct|^\alpha (1 - i\beta\,\mathrm{sign}(t)\,\omega_\alpha(t))\big)$, with $\omega_\alpha(t) = \tan(\pi\alpha/2)$ for $\alpha \ne 1$, $\omega_1(t) = -\tfrac{2}{\pi}\log|t|$, and $0 < \alpha \le 2$, $c \ge 0$, $|\beta| \le 1$, $\mu \in \mathbb{R}$.

hypotheses.text: The law is [stable](c:stable-distribution): for every $n$, the sum of $n$ [independent](c:independent-random-variables) copies $X_1, \dots, X_n$ has the law of $a_n X_1 + b_n$ with $a_n > 0$ and $b_n \in \mathbb{R}$.
In the formula $0 < \alpha \le 2$, $c \ge 0$, $|\beta| \le 1$ and $\mu \in \mathbb{R}$.

conclusion: The [stable](c:stable-distribution) laws are exactly the laws with this [characteristic function](c:characteristic-function). A stable law that is not a point mass has $c > 0$ and norming constants $a_n = n^{1/\alpha}$.

proofs.name: Through the functional equation and tail balance
proofs.slogan: Solve the functional equation of the characteristic function, then bound the skewness constant through the balance of the two tails.
proofs.scope: The full equivalence. The sufficiency rests on the Lévy–Khintchine formula, and the bound on the skewness constant rests on the cited tail estimates in Sections 6-7 of the source.

roles.why: Stability gives the functional equation $\varphi(t)^n = \varphi(a_n t)e^{ib_n t}$, which the necessity steps solve.
The sufficiency step needs these bounds to build a Lévy measure, and the necessity steps prove that they hold.

steps.slogan: An explicit Lévy measure makes each formula the characteristic function of a stable law.
steps.detail: For $0 < \alpha < 2$ the [Lévy measure](c:levy-measure) $[(1-\beta)1(x<0) + (1+\beta)1(x>0)]\,c^\alpha dx/(2K(\alpha)|x|^{1+\alpha})$ with $K(\alpha) = -\Gamma(-\alpha)\cos(\pi\alpha/2)$ gives the exponent up to a drift. The Lévy–Khintchine formula makes it a characteristic function, and $n\psi_{\alpha,c,\beta,\mu} = \psi_{\alpha,n^{1/\alpha}c,\beta,n\mu}$ gives stability.

steps.slogan: The functional equation forces power norming constants and a characteristic function without zeros.
steps.detail: From $\varphi(t)^n = \varphi(a_n t)e^{ib_n t}$ one gets $1 = a_1 < a_2 < \cdots$, $a_{mn} = a_m a_n$, $b_m(n - a_n) = b_n(m - a_m)$ and $\varphi(t) \ne 0$. A strictly increasing multiplicative sequence is $a_n = n^{1/\alpha}$.

steps.slogan: For index different from one, the shifted logarithm is homogeneous of degree alpha.
steps.detail: With $b_n = \gamma(n - n^{1/\alpha})$ the function $\psi_0 = \log\varphi - i\gamma t$ satisfies $\psi_0(rt) = r^\alpha \psi_0(t)$ for $r, t > 0$. Conjugation gives $\log\varphi(t) = i\gamma t - c|t|^\alpha(1 - ic'\,\mathrm{sign}(t))$ with $c > 0$.

steps.slogan: For index one, the drift correction is a logarithm, which gives the term in t log t.
steps.detail: The numbers $B_r$ in $r\log\varphi(t) = \log\varphi(rt) + iB_r rt$ satisfy $B_{rs} = B_r + B_s$ and are continuous, so $B_r = \lambda\log r$. This gives $\log\varphi(t) = iyt - c(t + ic't\log t)$ for $t > 0$.

steps.slogan: A second-moment argument excludes an index above two.
steps.detail: Since $1 - \mathrm{Re}\,\varphi(t) \sim c|t|^\alpha$ and $2(1 - \mathrm{Re}\,\varphi(t))/t^2 \to E[X^2]$, an index $\alpha > 2$ gives $E[X^2] = 0$. Then $X$ has mean 0 and [variance](c:variance) 0, so the law is a point mass, which is a contradiction.

steps.slogan: Tail balance through regular variation bounds the skewness constant by one.
steps.detail: The real and imaginary parts of $\varphi$ near 0 are [regularly varying](c:regularly-varying-function) and control the tail sum $H$ and the tail difference $K$. steps.slogan: Rename the constants to get the canonical form and close both directions.

new_concepts.name: infinitely divisible distribution
new_concepts.reminder: An infinitely divisible law is, for every $n$, the law of a sum of $n$ iid random variables.
new_concepts.definition: A [probability distribution](c:probability-distribution) $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$ is infinitely divisible when for every $n\ge1$ there is a probability distribution $\mu_n$ with $\mu=\mu_n^{*n}$, the $n$-fold [convolution](c:convolution) power. Equivalently, for every $n$, a random variable with law $\mu$ has the law of $Y_{n,1}+\dots+Y_{n,n}$ with [iid random variables](c:iid-random-variables) $Y_{n,k}$. The Lévy–Khintchine formula describes all such laws by a drift, a Gaussian covariance and a [Lévy measure](c:levy-measure).

new_concepts.name: Levy measure
new_concepts.reminder: The Lévy measure $\nu(A)$ is the expected number of jumps per unit time of a Lévy process with size in $A$.
new_concepts.definition:
A Lévy measure on $\mathbb{R}^d$ is a [measure](c:measure) $
u$ on $\mathbb{R}^d\setminus\{0\}$ with $\int\min(1,|x|^2)\,
u(dx)<\infty$. In the Lévy–Khintchine formula for an [infinitely divisible distribution](c:infinitely-divisible-distribution) or a [Lévy process](c:levy-process) $X$, it describes the jumps: $
u(A)=\mathbb{E}[\#\{s\le1:\Delta X_s\in A\}]$ for each Borel set $A$ at positive distance from $0$. It can have infinite total mass near $0$, which means infinitely many small jumps.

new_concepts.name: regularly varying function
new_concepts.reminder: A regularly varying function grows like a power $x^\rho$ times a slowly varying factor at infinity.
new_concepts.definition: A positive [measurable function](c:measurable-function) $f$ on $(0,\infty)$ is regularly varying at infinity with index $\rho\in\mathbb{R}$ when $\lim_{x\to\infty}f(\lambda x)/f(x)=\lambda^\rho$ for every $\lambda>0$. Every such $f$ has the form $f(x)=x^\rho L(x)$, where $L$ is a [slowly varying function](c:slowly-varying-function).

new_concepts.name: stable distribution
new_concepts.reminder: A stable law keeps its type under sums: a sum of iid copies is an affine image of one copy.
new_concepts.definition: A nondegenerate law $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is stable when for every $n\ge1$ there are $a_n>0$ and $b_n\in\mathbb{R}$ such that, for [iid random variables](c:iid-random-variables) $X,X_1,\dots,X_n$ with law $\mu$, the sum $X_1+\dots+X_n$ has the law of $a_nX+b_n$. Then $a_n=n^{1/\alpha}$ for an index $\alpha\in(0,2]$, and the index $\alpha=2$ gives the normal laws. statement: Let $X_1, X_2, \dots$ be [i.i.d.](c:iid-random-variables) with $P(|X_1| > x) = x^{-\alpha}L(x)$, $0 < \alpha < 2$, $L$ [slowly varying](c:slowly-varying-function), and $P(X_1 > x)/P(|X_1| > x) \to \theta$. With $a_n = \inf\{x : P(|X_1|>x) \le 1/n\}$ and $b_n = n\mathbb{E}[X_1; |X_1| \le a_n]$, $(S_n - b_n)/a_n$ [converges in distribution](c:convergence-in-distribution) to a nondegenerate [stable](c:stable-distribution) $Y$ with [Lévy measure](c:levy-measure) $\nu(dx) = \theta\alpha x^{-\alpha-1}dx$ on $x>0$ and $(1-\theta)\alpha|x|^{-\alpha-1}dx$ on $x<0$.

hypotheses.text: The variables $X_1, X_2, \dots$ are [i.i.d.](c:iid-random-variables)
The tail $T(x) = P(|X_1| > x)$ is [regularly varying](c:regularly-varying-function) with index $-\alpha$, $0 < \alpha < 2$.
The right tail carries the fraction $\theta \in [0,1]$ of the total tail: $P(X_1 > x)/T(x) \to \theta$.

conclusion: $(S_n - b_n)/a_n$ [converges in distribution](c:convergence-in-distribution) to a nondegenerate $Y$ with $\mathbb{E}e^{itY} = \exp\int (e^{itx} - 1 - itx 1_{|x|\le 1})\,\nu(dx)$.

proofs.name: Direct characteristic function computation
proofs.slogan: Scale so that one jump exceeds $a_n$ about once, control small values by a halving bound, and take the limit of $n(\chi_n - 1)$.
proofs.scope: Sufficiency for $0 < \alpha < 2$.

roles.why: Identical independent summands make the [characteristic function](c:characteristic-function) of $S_n/a_n$ an $n$-th power.
Regular variation gives $nT(xa_n) \to x^{-\alpha}$ and the halving bound, and $\alpha < 2$ makes the small values negligible.
Tail balance splits the limit of $nP(X_1/a_n \in \cdot)$ into the two half-line densities of $\nu$.

steps.slogan: The scale $a_n$ makes the expected number of large values converge.
steps.detail: From $T(a_n) \le 1/n < T(a_n/\lambda)$ and regular variation, $nT(a_n) \to 1$, so $nP(X_1 > xa_n) \to \theta x^{-\alpha}$ and $nP(X_1 < -xa_n) \to (1-\theta)x^{-\alpha}$.

steps.slogan: Repeated halving gives a uniform power bound on tail ratios.
steps.detail: With $T(s/2) \le 2^{\alpha+\delta}T(s)$ for $s \ge t_0$, iteration gives $T(yt) \le C y^{-\alpha-\delta}T(t)$ for all $t \ge t_0$ and $0 < y \le 1$.

steps.slogan: Values below $\varepsilon a_n$ carry a small total second moment.
steps.detail: $n\mathbb{E}[(X_1/a_n)^2; |X_1| \le \varepsilon a_n] \le \int_0^\varepsilon 2y\,nT(ya_n)\,dy \le K\varepsilon^{2-\alpha-\delta}$, which tends to 0 with $\varepsilon$ because $\alpha + \delta < 2$.

steps.slogan: The exponent $n(\chi_n - 1) - itn\beta_n$ converges to $\int h_t\,d\nu$.
steps.detail: Weak convergence of $nP(X_1/a_n \in \cdot)$ away from 0 handles $|x| > \varepsilon$. The bound $|h_t(x)| \le t^2x^2/2$ and the small-value estimate handle $|x| \le \varepsilon$.

steps.slogan: Compare the $n$-th power with an exponential.
steps.detail: Cauchy–Schwarz gives $n\beta_n^2 \to 0$, so $n|\chi_n - 1|^2 \to 0$ and $|\chi_n^n - e^{n(\chi_n - 1)}| \le n|\chi_n - 1|^2 \to 0$. Hence $\mathbb{E}e^{itZ_n} \to e^{\psi(t)}$.

steps.slogan: Continuity at 0 identifies a nondegenerate limit law.
steps.detail: Dominated convergence makes $\psi$ continuous at 0, and Lévy's continuity theorem gives $Z_n \Rightarrow Y$. Since $\operatorname{Re}\psi(t) < 0$ for $t \ne 0$, $Y$ is not constant.

statement: Let $X_1, X_2, \dots$ be [i.i.d.](c:iid-random-variables) and not constant, with $T(y) = P(|X_1| > y)$ and $U(y) = \mathbb{E}[X_1^2; |X_1| \le y]$. proofs.name: Truncation for sufficiency, symmetrization for necessity
proofs.slogan: Truncate at the scale where $nU(a_n) = a_n^2$ for sufficiency, and use symmetrization to show that a Gaussian limit leaves no room for large values.
proofs.scope: Both directions for nondegenerate $X_1$.

roles.why: Identical independent summands make the truncated array satisfy the Lindeberg–Feller hypotheses, and make the [characteristic function](c:characteristic-function) of the symmetrized sum a power $\psi(t/a_n)^n$.
A nondegenerate $X_1$ forces $a_n \to \infty$ and gives $U(y) > 0$ for large $y$.

steps.slogan: Truncate at the scale with $nU(a_n) = a_n^2$ and apply Lindeberg–Feller.
steps.detail: The condition makes $U$ [slowly varying](c:slowly-varying-function). With $nU(a_n) = a_n^2$, truncation at $a_n$ changes $S_n$ with probability at most $nT(a_n) \to 0$, the centered truncated [triangular array](c:triangular-array) has variance sum tending to 1, and slow variation gives the Lindeberg condition.

steps.slogan: Symmetrize, get uniform convergence of the characteristic functions, and show $a_n \to \infty$.
steps.detail: With $X^s = X_1 - X'_1$ and $\psi = |\varphi|^2$, $\psi(t/a_n)^n \to e^{-t^2}$ uniformly on compacts by tightness. A bounded subsequence of $a_n$ would force $\psi \equiv 1$ and a constant $X_1$.

steps.slogan: An algebraic identity kills the large values of $X^s$.
steps.detail: With $f_n(t) = n(1 - \psi(t/a_n)) \to t^2$, the identity $2(1-\cos x)^2 = 4(1 - \cos x) - (1 - \cos 2x)$ gives $n\mathbb{E}[2(1 - \cos(tX^s/a_n))^2] \to 0$. Integrating in $t$ yields $nP(|X^s| > \varepsilon a_n) \to 0$.

steps.slogan: The truncated second moment of $X^s$ matches the Gaussian variance.
steps.detail: Expanding $1 - \cos y = y^2/2 - r(y)$ gives $n\mathbb{E}[(X^s)^2; |X^s| \le \varepsilon a_n]/a_n^2 \to 2$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$.

steps.slogan: Bounded ratios $a_{n+1}/a_n$ pass from the sequence $a_n$ to all large $y$.
steps.detail: If $a_{n+1}/a_n$ were unbounded, the moment limit would fail at $n+1$. For $a_n \le y < a_{n+1}$, $y^2T^s(y)/U^s(y) \le K^2 nT^s(a_n)/(nU^s(a_n)/a_n^2) \to 0$.

steps.slogan: Return from $X^s$ to $X_1$ through a [median](c:median).
steps.detail: With $Y = X_1 - m$, $P(|Y| > y) \le 2T^s(y)$ and $U^s(y) \le 4\mathbb{E}[\min(Y^2, y^2)]$ transfer the condition to $Y$, and a shift by $m$ changes $T$ and $U$ only by constant factors at scale $y/2$.

new_concepts.reminder: A triangular array has rows of random variables that are independent within each row, with row lengths that grow.
new_concepts.definition: A triangular array is a family of real [random variables](c:random-variable) $X_{n,k}$, $n\ge1$, $1\le k\le k_n$, with $k_n\to\infty$, such that for each $n$ the variables $X_{n,1},\dots,X_{n,k_n}$ of row $n$ are [independent](c:independent-random-variables). statement: A nondegenerate [random variable](c:random-variable) $Y$ is the limit in distribution of $(X_1 + \dots + X_n - b_n)/a_n$ for some [i.i.d.](c:iid-random-variables) sequence and constants $a_n > 0$, $b_n$ if and only if $Y$ has a [stable distribution](c:stable-distribution): $Y_1 + \dots + Y_k \overset{d}{=} \alpha_k Y + \beta_k$ for every $k$, with i.i.d. copies $Y_j$ of $Y$ and some $\alpha_k > 0$, $\beta_k$.

hypotheses.text: $Y$ is a [random variable](c:random-variable) that is not almost surely constant.
The summands $X_i$ are [i.i.d.](c:iid-random-variables), and the normalization uses constants $a_n > 0$ and $b_n \in \mathbb{R}$.

conclusion: $Y$ is a limit of normalized sums of an i.i.d. sequence exactly when $Y$ has a [stable distribution](c:stable-distribution).

proofs.name: Blocks and convergence of types
proofs.slogan: Group $nk$ summands into $k$ blocks of length $n$, and let convergence of types turn the two limits of the same sum into a stability relation.
proofs.scope: The whole equivalence for nondegenerate limits.

roles.why: Convergence of types needs two different quantiles, so both $Y$ and $Y_1 + \dots + Y_k$ must be nondegenerate.
Identical laws make the $k$ blocks independent copies of $S_n$, and positive scales make quantiles transform as $q_{\alpha V + \beta} = \alpha q_V + \beta$.

steps.slogan: A stable law is the limit of its own normalized sums.
steps.detail: If $Y$ is stable, take $X_i$ i.i.d. copies of $Y$ with $a_n = \alpha_n$ and $b_n = \beta_n$. Then every normalized sum already has the law of $Y$.

steps.slogan: Convergence in distribution moves quantiles at their continuity points.
steps.detail: If $V_n \Rightarrow V$ and the quantile function $q_V$ of the [distribution function](c:distribution-function) is continuous at $y$, then $q_{V_n}(y) \to q_V(y)$. The proof squeezes $q_{V_n}(y)$ between two continuity points of $F$.

steps.slogan: Two quantiles fix the scale and the shift of an affine image.
steps.detail: If $W_n \Rightarrow W$ and $\alpha_n W_n + \beta_n \Rightarrow W'$ with both limits nondegenerate, then the quantiles at two good points $y_1 < y_2$ force $\alpha_n \to \alpha > 0$ and $\beta_n \to \beta$, and $W' \overset{d}{=} \alpha W + \beta$.

steps.slogan: Split $S_{nk}$ into $k$ independent blocks of length $n$.
steps.detail: The normalized block sums give $W'_n \Rightarrow Y_1 + \dots + Y_k$ by [characteristic functions](c:characteristic-function), and the same quantity equals $(a_{nk}/a_n) Z_{nk} + (b_{nk} - k b_n)/a_n$ with $Z_{nk} \Rightarrow Y$.

steps.slogan: Convergence of types turns the two limits into the stability relation.
steps.detail: The sum $Y_1 + \dots + Y_k$ is nondegenerate, so convergence of types gives $Y_1 + \dots + Y_k \overset{d}{=} \alpha_k Y + \beta_k$ with $\alpha_k > 0$. Together with the easy direction this proves the equivalence.
